games.title: The Heme and Liver: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following is the primary site of heme synthesis in adults?
questions.explanation: In adults, about 85 % of heme synthesis occurs in the bone marrow, with the liver accounting for the remainder.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of acute hepatic failure in patients with chronic alcoholism?
questions.explanation: Alcoholic hepatitis is the leading cause of acute hepatic failure among chronic alcohol users.

questions.q: Which enzyme deficiency leads to porphyria cutanea tarda, characterized by photosensitivity and blistering?
questions.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda.

questions.q: In the context of liver function tests, a markedly elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) with a normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: ALT elevation with normal ALP suggests hepatocellular injury rather than cholestasis.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of Wilson disease?
questions.explanation: Elevated serum alkaline phosphatase is not a classic feature of Wilson disease; the disease is characterized by Kayser‑Fleischer rings, hemolytic anemia, and low ceruloplasmin.

questions.q: The most sensitive laboratory test for detecting acute hepatic necrosis is:
questions.explanation: Serum ALT rises earlier and is more specific for hepatocellular necrosis.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of bilirubin conjugation in the liver?
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes conjugate bilirubin with glucuronic acid via UDP‑glucuronosyltransferase.

questions.q: In a patient with chronic hepatitis C, which of the following is the most appropriate first‑line antiviral therapy?
questions.explanation: Sofosbuvir plus ledipasvir is a highly effective direct‑acting antiviral regimen for HCV.

questions.q: Which of the following is a major risk factor for developing hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: All listed conditions are independent risk factors for HCC in cirrhosis.

questions.q: The ratio of prothrombin time (PT) to international normalized ratio (INR) is used to monitor which of the following treatments?
questions.explanation: PT/INR monitoring is essential for patients on warfarin to maintain therapeutic anticoagulation.

games.title: Chemicals and pesticides: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 42‑year‑old woman presents with a 3‑day history of nausea, vomiting, and a metallic taste. She reports that she was gardening yesterday and used a commercial herbicide containing glyphosate. Examination shows mild tachycardia and a dry mucous membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glyphosate causes GI upset and metallic taste; organophosphates give cholinergic signs.

questions.q: A 27‑year‑old farmer develops sudden onset of muscle weakness, difficulty swallowing, and a dry cough after handling a spray containing chlorpyrifos. His pupils are pinpoint. Which antidote should be administered first?
questions.explanation: Organophosphate toxicity is treated first with atropine to counter muscarinic effects.

questions.q: A 55‑year‑old man presents with a 2‑week history of fatigue, weight loss, and a diffuse rash. He works in a pesticide factory and reports frequent exposure to organochlorine pesticides. Which laboratory finding would most support the diagnosis of chronic organochlorine poisoning?
questions.explanation: Chronic organochlorine exposure leads to low serum cholinesterase levels.

questions.q: A 35‑year‑old woman presents with sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and a left-sided hemiparesis. She reports that she was applying a pesticide containing paraquat to her garden 12 hours ago. What is the next best step in management?
options: A. Immediate whole‑body decontamination and supportive care
questions.explanation: Paraquat causes pulmonary toxicity; early decontamination and supportive care are essential.

questions.q: A 60‑year‑old man presents with a 1‑month history of progressive memory loss and gait instability. He works as a pesticide applicator and has been exposed to organophosphates for 30 years. Which imaging finding is most characteristic of chronic organophosphate neurotoxicity?
options: A. Bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensity on T2 MRI
B. Diffuse cortical atrophy on CT
C. White matter hyperintensities on MRI
questions.explanation: Chronic organophosphate exposure is associated with white matter changes.

questions.q: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with burning pain in her eyes, throat, and skin after handling a new pesticide product. Her pupils are dilated and she has a dry cough. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Organophosphate poisoning presents with muscarinic symptoms; atropine is first line.

questions.q: A 48‑year‑old man presents with a 2‑day history of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and a metallic taste. He reports that he cleaned a pesticide container with a solvent. Which laboratory test would most likely be abnormal?
questions.explanation: Organophosphate poisoning can cause hyperkalemia due to cellular leakage.

questions.q: A 30‑year‑old woman presents with sudden onset of blurred vision, headache, and a metallic taste after using a new herbicide. Her pupils are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glyphosate exposure causes metallic taste and GI symptoms without cholinergic signs.

games.title: Post-operative Care and Complications of Surgery: drug duel
games.topic: Post-operative Care and Complications of Surgery
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which drug is most commonly used to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting in patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
questions.explanation: Ondansetron, a 5‑HT3 antagonist, is the first‑line antiemetic for postoperative nausea and vomiting.

questions.q: What is the mechanism of action of tranexamic acid in reducing postoperative bleeding after cardiac surgery?
options: B) Inhibition of fibrinolysis by lysine‑binding to plasminogen
C) Activation of the coagulation cascade
questions.explanation: Tranexamic acid blocks lysine sites on plasminogen, preventing fibrin clot breakdown.

questions.q: Which drug is indicated for prophylaxis against deep vein thrombosis in patients after hip replacement surgery?
questions.explanation: Low‑molecular‑weight heparin (enoxaparin) is the standard prophylaxis for DVT after hip arthroplasty.

questions.q: What is the characteristic side effect of cefazolin when used for prophylaxis in abdominal surgery?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin can cause a type I hypersensitivity rash, especially in patients with a β‑lactam allergy.

questions.q: Which drug is most appropriate to treat postoperative pain after thoracotomy when the patient has a history of asthma?
questions.explanation: Fentanyl is a short‑acting opioid with minimal respiratory depression, suitable for asthmatic patients.

questions.q: What is the main indication for administering dexamethasone intraoperatively in patients undergoing major abdominal surgery?
options: A) Reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting
D) Reduce postoperative edema and inflammation
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone decreases postoperative inflammation and edema, improving recovery.

questions.q: Which drug is contraindicated in patients with a history of pancreatitis undergoing postoperative care after pancreaticoduodenectomy?
questions.explanation: Ketorolac, a potent NSAID, can precipitate pancreatitis and is contraindicated.

questions.q: What is the mechanism of action of droperidol in preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting?
questions.explanation: Droperidol blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, reducing nausea.

games.title: Anemia of Inadequate production: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which drug is most commonly used to treat iron‑deficiency anemia in children with inadequate erythropoiesis?
questions.explanation: Ferrous sulfate is the first‑line oral iron supplement for iron‑deficiency anemia.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of recombinant human erythropoietin in treating anemia of inadequate production?
options: A. Stimulates iron absorption in the gut
B. Increases red cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis
C. Stimulates erythroid progenitor proliferation in the bone marrow
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin binds to erythroid progenitors, promoting their proliferation and differentiation.

questions.q: Which side effect is most characteristic of high‑dose iron therapy in children?
options: C. Iron overload leading to hepatotoxicity
questions.explanation: Excess iron can accumulate in the liver, causing hepatotoxicity and cirrhosis.

questions.q: Which drug is indicated for anemia of chronic disease in children when iron therapy is ineffective?
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is used when iron deficiency is not the cause of anemia.

questions.q: What is the most common adverse effect of hydroxyurea used in sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea can cause dose‑dependent myelosuppression.

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency can lead to megaloblastic anemia in children?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia due to impaired DNA synthesis.

questions.q: Which drug is used to treat anemia of chronic kidney disease in children when erythropoietin therapy fails?
questions.explanation: Recombinant human erythropoietin analogs (e.g., darbepoetin) are used when standard erythropoietin is ineffective.

questions.q: What is the main indication for folic acid supplementation in paediatric anemia?
options: C. Reducing hemolysis in sickle cell disease
questions.explanation: Folic acid is indicated for folate‑deficiency anemia, which can cause macrocytosis.
